# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-7 (Extended v83)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 2, approximately late 1825 or late 1826)**: Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary at Convent of Petit-Picpus. Key dates: 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, Valjean's theft and flight; Waterloo/Hougomont June 17-18); 1817 (young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral tenure); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest; Javert's revelation; TRIAL SEQUENCE in Arras; Valjean's self-revelation; acquittal of Champmathieu; RETURN TO M. SUR M. before six a.m.; Fantine's death; Valjean arrested beside death-bed; VALJEAN ESCAPES same evening)**; December 1823 (Montfermeil rescue of Cosette, 1,500-franc payment to Thénardier); **December 26, 1823 (Valjean and Cosette returned to Paris via Barrier Monceaux)**; 1824 spring onward (decrepit building lodging; winter passed; spring advanced); **Summer Year 2**: Achieved sanctuary inside walled garden compound, le Petit-Picpus district. **1819-1825 (Six-year span during Prioress Mademoiselle de Blemeur's tenure)**. **1820 or 1821 (Madame de Genlis's brief residence attempt)**. **1824 (Nun of Sainte-Aure's death; only doll of her order remains)**. **1845**: Order received no professed nun recruits, only lay-sisters; convent abandoned education of girls. **1847 (Mother Présentation became prioress at age under forty)**.

## Primary Locations
M. sur M.; Montfermeil (between Livry and Chelles); **English harbor towns** (Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Ravenmere, Staveford); Arras; Waterloo; Toulon; Paris districts including Mouffetard quarter (Rue Censier, Rue Copeau, Rue du Battoir-Saint-Victor, Rue du Puits l'Ermite, Rue de Pontoise; commissary office No. 14; Saint-Étienne-du-Mont church); **Gorbeau House** (Rue de la Cosette area, Mouffetard): Decrepit lodging, old woman portress, Javert's surveillance station. **Mouffetard escape**: Street lantern rope cut; Javert misled toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; market-gardens, timber-yards, unpaved roads; ancient street names (Droit-Mur formerly Rue des Églantiers; Aumarais formerly Maugout Lane). **Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (CONVENT CARRIAGE GATE)**: Ajar gate, courtyard, vine-hung walls, tall trees above wall. **Wall (approximately 18 feet)**: Extends from niche to house 49 Rue Polonceau; shorter fragment along Rue Droit-Mur. **CONVENT COMPLEX - THREE BUILDINGS**: (1) **Great Convent**: Inhabited by Bernardines-Benedictines nuns; gloomy building, heavily shuttered window with sheet zinc, ancient cistern pipes, linden-tree with ivy, grated windows, upper story scuttles resembling prison cells. (2) **Boarding-school**: Where scholars lodged. (3) **Little Convent**: Building with garden housing aged nuns of various orders destroyed in Revolution. **INTERIOR GARDEN (Great Convent)**: Vast oblong area; alley of large poplars; forest trees in corners; solitary gnarled tree, fruit-trees, vegetable beds, melon patch with glass frames, old well, stone benches, grass and green mould. **PARLOR (Great Convent)**: Theatre-box-like narrow space; monstrous lattice of iron bars (squares less than 1.5 inches diagonal) riveted by clenched-fist fastenings; behind lattice: barrier of black shutters reinforced with gingerbread-yellow wooden beams, always closed; behind shutters: nun's voice screened by iron grating and plate with thousand holes; slat opens revealing nun's mouth and chin only, covered with black veil, guimpe, shroud; window on world-side only; quadrangular hole one foot square with interlacing iron bars reinforced by sheet of tin with thousand microscopic holes; tape attached to bell-wire.

## Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration
**Order Lineage**: Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga obedience; **1657 (Pope Alexander VII authorized Bernardines of Rue Petit-Picpus to practice Perpetual Adoration like Benedictine nuns of Holy Sacrament); two orders remained distinct**. Benedictine order founded 529 by Saint-Benoît; spawned nine orders. **Dress**: Black clothing with white guimpe; serge robe with large sleeves; large woollen veil; novices wear all-white; professed nuns wear rosary at side. **Austerity**: Fast all year; abstain from meat; additional fasting in Lent; rise one to three a.m. for breviary and matins; sleep year-round on straw between serge sheets; never light fires; never bathe; scourge every Friday; strict silence except brief recreation; wear drugget chemises September 14 to Easter—originally year-round but modified due to summer fevers. **Vows**: Obedience, poverty, chastity, perseverance in seclusion. **Operational Rules**: Never see officiating priest (hidden behind nine-foot serge curtain); drop veils during sermons; speak low; walk with eyes down; only diocesan archbishop permitted entry; absolute passive submission to prioress (canonical subjection—at Christ's voice, at gesture, at first sign, immediately with cheerfulness, perseverance, blind obedience); cannot read or write without express permission. **Reparation Practice**: Each nun in turn performs twelve-hour continuous reparation prayer on knees on stone before Holy Sacrament, hands clasped, rope around neck; when fatigue unbearable, prostrates flat against earth, arms outstretched as cross. **Possessions Rule**: Never say "my"; call everything "our". **Hourly Bells**: At each hour three supplementary church bell strokes; all interrupt activity and say formula praising Most Holy Sacrament. **Chanting**: Solemn psalmody, pure Gregorian chant, full voice; for office of dead adopt tone so low women's voices can barely descend—effect striking and tragic. **Burial Issue**: Vault beneath grand altar for community burials; Government forbids coffin burial in vault, so nuns leave convent when die. **Convent Communication System—Bell-Telegraph Network**: Rule of silence withdrew speech from human creatures; speech bestowed on inanimate objects—church-bell and gardener's bell. Sonorous bell beside portress, audible throughout house, indicated by varied peals (acoustic telegraph) all material-life actions to be performed. Each person and thing had own peal: prioress one-and-one; sub-prioress one-and-two; six-five announced lessons; four-four was Madame de Genlis's signal. **Nine strokes announced great event: opening of door of seclusion—frightful sheet of iron bristling with bolts, turned on hinges only in presence of archbishop**. **Men Allowed in Convent (Three Only)**: Archbishop, chaplain Abbé Banés, drawing-master M. Ansiaux/Anciot.

## Prioress and Vocal Mothers (1819-1825 Period)
**Mademoiselle de Blemeur (Mother Innocente)** (Prioress, 1819-1825): Age ~sixty; short, thick; "singing like a cracked pot"; excellent woman; only merry one in convent, adored for this; learned, erudite, wise, competent; proficient in history; crammed with Latin, Greek, Hebrew; more Benedictine monk than nun; descended from Marguerite de Blemeur, author of _Lives of the Saints of the Order of Saint-Benoît_; re-elected. **Vocal Mothers**: Mother Sainte-Honorine; Mother Sainte-Gertrude (treasurer); Mother-Saint-Ange; Mother Annonciation (sacristan); Mother Saint-Augustin (nurse; only malicious one); Mother Sainte-Mechtilde (Mademoiselle Gauvain; very young; beautiful voice; directs singing); Mother des Anges (Mademoiselle Drouet); Mother Saint-Joseph (Mademoiselle de Cogolludo); Mother Sainte-Adélaide (Mademoiselle d'Auverney); Mother Miséricorde (Mademoiselle de Cifuentes); Mother Compassion (Mademoiselle de la Miltière); Mother Providence (Mademoiselle de Laudinière); Mother Présentation (Mademoiselle de Siguenza; future prioress 1847); Mother Sainte-Céligne; Mother Sainte-Chantal. **Order Decline**: Forty years before 1845, nuns numbered nearly a hundred; fifteen years before 1845 (circa 1830), not more than twenty-eight; by 1845, none at all professed nuns, only lay-sisters; as numbers diminish, fatigue increases, service of each becomes more painful; death rate rises—two died during author's Paris residence (ages twenty-five and twenty-three); burden implacable and crushes few as heavily as many.

## Resident Women in Little Convent
**Madame Albertine**: Woman not a nun, ~thirty years old; dark complexion; tolerably pretty; passed for dead in world; vague look in large black eyes; could she see—doubt about this; glided rather than walked; never spoke; uncertain whether she breathed; possessed strange spectral grace; wherever she entered, people felt cold; touching her hand like touching snow. **Connection**: Once uttered "Ah! Auguste!" revealing knowledge of M. de Rohan (Vicar-general, awaiting episcopate); evident she belonged to very highest society. **Other Resident Women**: Madame Beaufort d'Hautpoul, Marquise Dufresne. **Centenarian from Abbey of Fontevrault**: Talked much of M. de Miromesnil and Presidentess Duplat; claimed in her youth Bernardine monks were as good as mousquetaires; spoke eighteenth century through her; told of custom of four wines in Champagne and Bourgogne before Revolution expressing four stages descended by drunkard: intoxication, irritation, dulling, brutalization. **Madame de Genlis** (attempted 1820-1821): Editing periodical _l'Intrépide_; requested residence; Duc d'Orléans recommended; declared self devoted; departed end of six or eight months, alleging no shade in garden; nuns delighted. **Nun of Sainte-Aure**: Only survivor of her order; **1824: only one nun of order remained; currently: only doll remains**.

## Jean Valjean's Current Sanctuary Status
**ESCAPE FROM M. SUR M.** (January 1823 evening): Successfully fled jail after Javert's arrest beside Fantine's death-bed; climbed 18-foot wall using muscular force; placed Cosette on back; descended safely to interior garden via roof. **REFUGE DISCOVERY AND FAUCHELEVENT**: Encountered elderly crippled gardener Fauchelevent, admitted to convent approximately two years previously (1821) on Mayor Madeleine's recommendation after falling from cart. **PSYCHOLOGICAL STATE**: So long as Cosette near, needs nothing except her, fears nothing except her; experiencing continual tremor. **COSETTE**: Now sleeping in Fauchelevent's bed; rosy; completely dependent on Valjean. **CURRENT LOCATION** (Autumn Year 2): Still secured in convent sanctuary. **ALTERED APPEARANCE**: Sadness, uneasiness, anxiety, depression have altered his walk and impressed senility on bearing.

## Fauchelevent (Elderly Gardener—Established Ally)
**Identity**: Old crippled gardener; admitted to convent approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; calls Valjean "Father Madeleine"; speaks freely about work. **Current Occupation**: Spreading straw mats over melon beds in garden; wears bell and kneecap device. **Hospitality**: Provided Cosette safe bed; offered cheese, black bread, wine. **Status**: Valjean's only known ally and protector in Paris; sole person aware of Valjean and Cosette's presence.

## Javert's Pursuit and Strategic Hesitation
**REASSIGNMENT TO PARIS** (January 1823): When Valjean escaped M. sur M. jail, Javert summoned; attached to Paris police force. **NEWSPAPER REPORT** (December 1823): Newspaper announced Valjean's death; Javert read, remarked "That's a good entry," thought no more. **REACTIVATION**: Police report concerning child abduction in Montfermeil revived Javert's memory; suspected Valjean had sought daughter. **JAVERT'S SECRET INVESTIGATION**: Without telling anyone, took coach to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; hired room, listened at lodger's door; Valjean foiled spy by silence. **REASONS FOR SECRECY** (Three Motives): (1) Slightest indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) Recapturing ex-convict reputed dead was magnificent success—feared being deprived; (3) Javert had taste for unforeseen—hated well-heralded successes, preferred elaborating masterpieces in dark, unveiling suddenly. **PURSUIT ESCALATION**: Following day Valjean noticed five-franc piece falling; old woman suspected lodger intending to leave, warned Javert; at night Javert waited behind trees with two men. **ESCAPE FROM MOUFFETARD**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder in lantern, led astray toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **JAVERT'S HESITATION AND PSYCHOLOGICAL TORMENT**: Followed Valjean from tree to tree, had not lost sight single instant; why had not arrested? Still in doubt. **STRATEGIC CALCULATION**: Considered abrupt demand for papers risky—if not Valjean, possibly chief of dangerous band; to arrest hastily would "kill the hen that laid golden eggs." Began the game—experienced ecstatic and infernal moment; allowed man to go ahead, knowing had him safe, gloating with voluptuousness of spider allowing fly to flutter. **MOMENT OF LOSS**: Even when saw Valjean escaped, Javert did not lose head; sure convict could not be far off, established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades. **IMPEDIMENT TO ARREST**: Free press embarrassed police; arbitrary arrests denounced by newspapers; interference with individual liberty grave matter; police agents afraid of mistakes; mistake meant dismissal.

## English Harbor Towns Communities (Secondary Setting—Recurring Pattern)
**Named residents**: Matho Stenson, Ismira Stenson, Pelde Stenson, Harine Lindmere, Davus Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Volia Brackick, Nelan Brackick, Kadrek Brackick, Rinelle Corrley, Lurald Stenworth, Volan Stenworth, Luwyn Brackick. **Towns/Locations**: Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Ravenmere, Staveford, Gulhaven, Kelmere pastures. **Key Fact**: In letter Lurald Stenworth revealed deed to Kelmere pastures was forged; letter burned by Nelan Brackick after reading. **Activities**: Reading almanacs aloud with mispronounced saints (Matho, Kadrek, Rinelle); sorting letters by candlelight (Rinelle); discussing weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices (Davus, Yera, Nelan, Rinelle, Kadrek); river up in spring (Harine, Orrald, Volan, Rinelle); aching back complaints (Davus, Kadrek); baker's boy late, line at oven long; rain threatening, then holding off; bees humming in lavender; frost silvering hedges; wind from water with salt and tar smell; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; children chased hoop down lane; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; ribbon bought and regretted (Nelan); argument with carter over sack of oats price (Harine); walking round to avoid muddy square (Pelde); mending torn sleeve by window (Harine); Orrald talked for weeks of going to Gulhaven, yet in end stayed where he was; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; light went early time of year. **Significant Event**: After quarrel, husband of Luwyn Brackick quit Kelford for good and took lodgings in Dunstead. **Atmosphere**: Recurring motif of weather, light, daily rhythms, quiet talk, minor regrets, small communities unchanging.
